title: Geopolitical energy shocks are narrowing growth and fiscal room unevenly, making debt capacity, buffers, and private investment central to social and institutional resilience
source_unit: World Bank Group, Global Economic Prospects, June 2026
geography: Global economy, emerging market and developing economies, low-income countries, commodity exporters, firms, households, and public budgets

observations.period: 2025-2028; global growth and geopolitical energy shock

denominator.unit: World Bank global economic outlook frame

downside_growth_2026.unit: percent projected global growth in a more severe disruption and financial-stress scenario in 2026

observations.method: World Bank global economic projections incorporating energy-price, conflict, trade, inflation, financial, and policy-risk scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: These are forecasts and downside scenarios, not realized outcomes; they depend on conflict duration, energy supply, financial stress, trade policy, substitution, and policy response.
observations.subgroup: Energy importers and exporters, households, firms, workers, governments, financial institutions, and economies with different fiscal and policy buffers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Energy prices and trade can recover faster than assumed, while policy support, substitution, strategic reserves, and private investment can cushion the aggregate slowdown; average growth hides distributional effects.

denominator.unit: emerging market and developing economy regional outlook frame

developing_economy_growth_2025.unit: percent growth in developing economies in 2025

developing_economy_growth_2026.unit: percent projected growth in developing economies in 2026

low_income_growth_2026.unit: percent projected growth in low-income countries in 2026

low_income_per_capita_growth_2026_2028.unit: percent average projected real per-capita GDP growth in low-income countries over 2026-2028

regional_exposure_mechanisms.value: energy exposure, strategic reserves, policy buffers, food and fertilizer prices, fiscal pressure, and financial conditions

observations.method: World Bank regional and low-income-country projections with analysis of energy exposure, reserves, policy buffers, commodity markets, and fiscal conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Regional averages do not identify country or household incidence; projections depend on conflict and commodity paths, domestic policy, weather, financing, and measurement revisions.
observations.subgroup: Low-income countries, commodity importers and exporters, food-insecure households, workers, firms, fiscal authorities, and economies with weak diversification.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some regions can maintain strong growth through domestic demand, diversification, reserves, remittances, or public investment even when global conditions weaken; per-capita averages do not establish poverty or welfare change.

observations.period: 2010-2026; sovereign debt, borrowing costs, and fiscal space

denominator.unit: emerging market and developing economy sovereign-finance frame

emde_debt_to_gdp_change.value: from under 40 percent to over 70 percent
emde_debt_to_gdp_change.unit: aggregate government-debt-to-GDP change in developing economies since 2010

sovereign_spread_association.unit: basis points associated with rising EMDE debt in sovereign spreads since 2010

domestic_currency_yield_association.unit: basis points associated with rising EMDE debt in domestic-currency yields since 2010

fiscal_space_endpoint.value: less room to respond to crises and invest in infrastructure, health, education, jobs, and social protection as debt service and borrowing costs rise

observations.method: World Bank analysis of sovereign debt, interest rates, spreads, domestic-currency yields, credit quality, governance, and fiscal-space implications.
observations.uncertainty: The associations are not a single causal estimate of debt on growth or welfare; debt composition, currency, maturity, monetary policy, growth, governance, and investor expectations all matter.
observations.subgroup: Highly indebted governments, public-service users, firms dependent on credit, workers, taxpayers, infrastructure providers, and creditors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Borrowing can finance productive investment and stabilize economies during shocks; debt reduction can create fiscal room only if adjustment protects essential services and does not deepen contraction.

observations.period: 2026; private investment, firms, infrastructure, and AI adoption

denominator.unit: emerging market and developing economy investment and productivity frame

private_investment_constraint_set.value: infrastructure gaps, high risk and uncertainty, and limited access to finance

investment_response.value: strengthening infrastructure, improving the business environment, expanding finance, and reinforcing institutional quality

ai_distribution_risk.value: economies without the ecosystem and policy environment to adopt AI widely risk falling further behind

jobs_endpoint.value: physical, human, and digital capital plus private investment are identified as routes to job creation

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of private-investment trends, firm constraints, AI adoption conditions, infrastructure, institutional quality, and job-creation policy.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies constraints and policy priorities, not realized firm investment, AI adoption, job quality, productivity, or equal access to capital and infrastructure.
observations.subgroup: Small and large firms, workers, governments, private investors, infrastructure providers, entrepreneurs, and communities outside high-capability locations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public and private investment can reinforce one another, and crisis conditions can accelerate reform or technology adoption; institutional reforms may take time and can distribute benefits unevenly.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank document page for the June 2026 Global Economic Prospects report and downloadable report.
World Bank press release with the growth, inflation, financing-response, debt, and regional outlook summary.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical-shock-to-growth-to-fiscal-space-to-investment route linking energy prices, inflation, debt, borrowing costs, public budgets, firms, infrastructure, AI adoption, and jobs. It is not respondent-level data, a household welfare estimate, a realized crisis outcome, or proof that fiscal or private-investment recommendations were implemented.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank Global Economic Prospects June 2026 landing page, document page, and press release were reviewed; global and regional forecasts, downside scenario, debt and borrowing-cost associations, private-investment constraints, AI risk, and policy-response boundaries were cross-checked.
